title: What six days cost
hook: Cases double every 3 days. Is a month of spread a few times bigger, or far more?

knows: a case can infect other people
doesNotKnow: how repeated doubling compounds over weeks
how a delay converts into extra doublings

misconception: Case growth is roughly linear, so a month of spread is a few times bigger and a few days of delay barely matter.
objective: The learner can convert a span of time into a number of doublings (30 days / 3 = 10, so x1,024) and explain that a 6-day delay with 3-day doubling multiplies cases by 4.

claims.text: 100 cases doubling every 3 days reach 100 x 2^10 = 102,400 after 30 days, about 100,000.
The last 3 days (day 27 to 30) added about as many cases as the first 27 days.
Going from day 30 back to day 24 cuts the count to a quarter (25,600): six days is two doublings, so a 6-day delay means four times as many cases.
The disease is made up and its doubling time never changes; each lit dot stands for 100 cases.
claims.source: Modelling choice in Demo.tsx (cases = 100 x 2^(day/3); 1,024 dots).

claims.text: Real outbreaks do not double forever: growth slows as people become immune or change how they mix.
claims.source: Kermack & McKendrick (1927), 'A contribution to the mathematical theory of epidemics', Proceedings of the Royal Society A 115: 700-721; Anderson & May (1991), Infectious Diseases of Humans, Oxford University Press.

recall.question: A count doubles every 4 days. Acting 8 days later than planned means about how many times as many cases at that moment?
recall.why: 8 days is 2 doublings at a 4-day doubling time, and 2 x 2 = 4.
